items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “movement of people across borders for the purpose of employment”.
items.answer: Labour migration
items.markingKey: Labour migration: movement of people across borders for the purpose of employment. [1]

items.stem: Explain the growth of labour migration to the Gulf states since the 1970s.
items.answer: Oil wealth after 1973 funded construction and services; small native populations; demand for labour in construction, domestic work and services; recruitment agencies in South and South-East Asia; wage differences of five to ten times.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor [4]

items.stem: Explain how remittances can contribute to development.
items.answer: Provide household income for food, education and health care; fund housing and small businesses; foreign exchange for the economy; more stable than aid or investment; but may increase inequality and dependency.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point [3]

items.stem: Table 15.1 shows approximate remittance inflows and GDP (US$ billion, 2023): Pakistan: remittances 27, GDP 338; Mexico: remittances 66, GDP 1 790; Tajikistan: remittances 5.7, GDP 12; India: remittances 120, GDP 3 550. Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP for each country.
items.answer: Pakistan 8%; Mexico 3.7%; Tajikistan 47.5%; India 3.4%
items.markingKey: remittances ÷ GDP × 100 [2]

items.stem: Table 15.1 shows approximate remittance inflows and GDP (US$ billion, 2023): Philippines: remittances 39, GDP 437; Nepal: remittances 11, GDP 41; Kyrgyzstan: remittances 2.6, GDP 14; Honduras: remittances 9.2, GDP 34. (a) Calculate remittances as a percentage of GDP for each country. (b) Explain why a country can receive large remittances but not be very dependent on them.
items.answer: (a) Philippines 8.9%; Nepal 26.8%; Kyrgyzstan 18.6%; Honduras 27.1% (b) A large economy (high GDP) means even large remittances are a small share of national income, e.g. India or Mexico.
items.markingKey: (a) remittances ÷ GDP × 100 [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: “International labour migration benefits source countries more than receiving countries.” Discuss. In your answer you may refer to remittances, social impacts and labour shortages.
items.answer: For: Remittances reduce poverty and fund development (Philippines, Nepal); emigration eases unemployment; returning migrants bring skills. Against: Receiving countries gain labour for construction, care and services and pay taxes (Gulf, UK, Germany); source countries suffer brain drain of doctors and nurses, ageing and family separation. Conclusion: Both gain economically, but receiving countries usually gain more in output while source countries gain income at a social cost.

items.stem: Explain the problems that labour migrants can face in destination countries.
items.answer: Exploitation and low pay; poor housing; restricted rights (kafala); debt to recruiters; discrimination; separation from families.

items.stem: Explain the causes of forced international migration.
items.answer: Armed conflict and civil war (Syria, Sudan, Ukraine); persecution of ethnic or religious groups (Rohingya); political repression; economic collapse (Venezuela); environmental disasters and climate change.

items.stem: Explain the impacts of large refugee inflows on host countries.
items.answer: Pressure on housing, water, schools and health care; competition for jobs; strain on public finances; possible tension; but labour, skills, consumer spending and international aid.

items.stem: Name a case study of forced international migration you have studied. For your example, explain the causes of the forced migration.
items.answer: the Rohingya from Myanmar: Long-term statelessness after the 1982 citizenship law; military violence in Rakhine State in August 2017 burnt hundreds of villages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Political, conflict, persecution, linked to places and dates. [5]

items.stem: Name a case study of forced international migration you have studied. For your example, describe the impacts on the host countries.
items.answer: the Rohingya from Myanmar: About 750 000 fled to Bangladesh in 2017; Kutupalong-Balukhali near Cox’s Bazar became the world’s largest refugee camp (about 1 million people); deforestation of hillsides, landslide risk; tension with host communities; relocation of some to Bhasan Char island.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Numbers, camps, services, economy, politics. [5]

items.answer: Model answer (Ukrainian refugees since 2022): Russian invasion of February 2022; bombardment of cities such as Kharkiv and Mariupol. About 6 million refugees, mostly women and children (men 18-60 were restricted from leaving); EU Temporary Protection Directive gave rights to work; Poland and Germany hosted about 1 million each; some return as fighting moved.

items.stem: Explain why many refugees remain in camps for many years.
items.answer: Conflict continues so return is unsafe; host countries restrict work and settlement; few resettlement places are offered by third countries.

items.stem: At the end of 2023, about 31.6 million refugees were under UNHCR’s mandate. Table 15.2 shows approximate numbers (millions) in selected host countries: Iran 3.8, Türkiye 3.3, Germany 2.6, Pakistan 2. Suggest why most of these hosts are neighbours of countries in conflict.
items.answer: Refugees flee to the nearest safe country on foot or by road; cultural and language ties; cost and legal barriers prevent longer journeys.

items.stem: Assess the view that the impacts of refugees on host countries are mainly negative. In your answer you may refer to integration and aid.
items.answer: For: Pressure on housing, water, health care and schools (Lebanon, Bangladesh); environmental damage near camps; political tension. Against: Refugees provide labour and skills, start businesses and consume goods (Syrians in Türkiye; Ukrainians in Poland); international aid flows in; long-term integration brings benefits. Conclusion: Short-term impacts in poor host countries are often negative, but with rights to work and support the long-term impacts can be positive.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that the costs of international migration are greater than the benefits for source countries?
items.answer: For: Brain drain of doctors and nurses (Zimbabwe, Philippines); ageing; family breakdown; labour shortages; dependency on remittances. Against: Remittances exceed aid and reduce poverty; reduced unemployment; return of skilled migrants; diaspora investment and trade links (India’s IT sector). Conclusion: For most source countries the economic benefits outweigh the costs, but the balance depends on how many skilled workers leave and how remittances are used.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A student writes: “Remittances to LICs and MICs are larger than official development aid.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) In a class discussion, a student says: “Most international migrants move from LICs to HICs.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Correct. Remittances to LMICs (about US$650 billion in 2023) are several times larger than aid. (b) Not correct. Many move between LICs or MICs (South-South migration), often to neighbouring countries.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) A revision website states: “Brain drain only affects the country of origin negatively.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain the growth of labour migration to the Gulf states since the 1970s.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Remittances, diaspora investment and returning skilled migrants can bring benefits (brain gain). (b) Oil wealth after 1973 funded construction and services; small native populations; demand for labour in construction, domestic work and services; recruitment agencies in South and South-East Asia; wage differences of five to ten times.

items.answer: A large economy (high GDP) means even large remittances are a small share of national income, e.g. India or Mexico.

items.stem: Arjun argues that international labour migration benefits source countries more than receiving countries. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples.
items.answer: For: Remittances reduce poverty and fund development (Philippines, Nepal); emigration eases unemployment; returning migrants bring skills. Against: Receiving countries gain labour for construction, care and services and pay taxes (Gulf, UK, Germany); source countries suffer brain drain of doctors and nurses, ageing and family separation. Conclusion: Both gain economically, but receiving countries usually gain more in output while source countries gain income at a social cost.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “diaspora”?
options: The presence and acceptance of several cultural or ethnic groups within a society.
People who have settled outside their country of origin but keep links with it.
The process by which migrants become part of the host society while keeping their own identity.
A lack of workers with the skills needed in particular sectors of the economy.
items.answer: People who have settled outside their country of origin but keep links with it.
